content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I read the paper at least twice and used my best judgement in assessing the paper.
content.review:
Paper proposes an approach for incremental learning where a network has to train new classes while not forgetting previously learned classes. 

The work in its current version is not ready for publication and I recommend rejection. 

- The proposed method is not clearly explained. The reader is referred to an algorithm for the explanation of the method. -No clear motivation for the method is provided in the introduction. 
-Work is not placed in context of lifelong learning literature (continual learning). 
-Text needs still serious editing. Still includes text like [reference of algorithm], and authors do not cite papers correctly (difference between cite and citep)
-The introduction only dedicates two lines on the proposed method, which were not clear for me. 
-It would be better if the training and evaluation protocol is explained before starting to explain the proposed architecture. What setting of incremental learning are the authors considering?

content.comment:
1. "The introduction only dedicates two lines on the proposed method, which were not clear for me."
Ans: We dedicated only a few lines to the proposed method in the introduction because we dedicated an entire section titled PROPOSED ARCHITECTURE for describing the proposed architecture in detail. We request you to refer to the PROPOSED ARCHITECTURE section where we described the algorithm both verbally and algorithmically. 

2. "It would be better if the training and evaluation protocol is explained before starting to explain the proposed architecture." 
Ans:  Since more than 3 metrics were used to evaluate the models and two different experiments were conducted to test them, describing all of them in the introduction demands a lot of valuable space. That is the reason we described everything in the EXPERIMENTAL SETUP section of the paper. There we explained the datasets used, models compared against and the experiments that were performed. Please refer to the EXPERIMENTAL SETUP section of the paper where we discussed everything in detail.

3. "What setting of incremental learning are the authors considering?"
Ans: The setting was described in the 4.3 EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS section. We considered two settings. (1) Incremental class learning (2) Multi-Modal learning. Please refer to section 4.3 EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS for a thorough explanation of the experiments.

4. "Text needs still serious editing. Still includes text like [reference of algorithm], and authors do not cite papers correctly (difference between cite and citep)"
Ans: Thank you for pointing them out. The errors mostly appear in the supplementary section. We will make sure to correct them before the final date. 

Thank you.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
The authors propose an ensemble model with deep networks. The authors suggest its relevance for incremental learning. The proposed model is evaluated appropriately. There are many issues with the work. The presentation and description needs a lot of improvement. 

What exactly do the authors mean by rehearsal? It is confusing term. "... architecture contains two layers of neural networks and only the neural network in final layer is exposed to rehearsal ...". Networks themselves have layers, so what does layers of networks mean here? The language needs a lot of improvement. 
Assuming that rehearsal means re-training or tuning or some sorts, the authors propose to split the network into two parts and retrain the second set of layers. How is this fundamentally different from retraining last few layers which is what most state of the art methods do? Further, architecture wise how is the proposal different from learning a layer of length C with softmax activation output for each class-specific index? What are we gaining in terms of learnability here?

As per description only a fraction of points from the rest of the classes are utilized as negative examples for learning a given class? This fraction seems very important/sensitive? What is its influence in evaluations? When a new class comes in in the form of incremental learning, one needs to retrain all the class specific models! Unlike claimed in the introduction, how is this small rehearsal or how is this different from retraining like in the conventional case?

In section 3.1, we still have a vector space, and nothing really special. Not need to tag them this separately!

For tables 2 and 3 we need confidence intervals for better interpreting the performance.

display_title: Thank you for your careful review, we request you to consider the arguments that we present in our defence.

content.title: Thank you for your careful review, we request you to consider the arguments that we present in our defence.
content.comment:
1. "What exactly do the authors mean by rehearsal?"
Ans: By rehearsal, we mean retraining the model with the old data.

2. "... architecture contains two layers of neural networks and only the neural network in final layer is exposed to rehearsal ...". Networks themselves have layers, so what does layers of networks mean here? 
Ans: Maybe we should have chosen the word "level" instead of "layers" to avoid confusion. Our proposed architecture has two "levels" of neural networks and the neural network that is present in the final level is retrained on the previous data. Please refer to Figure 1 in page number two for a pictorial representation of our architecture.

3. " the authors propose to split the network into two parts and retrain the second set of layers. How is this fundamentally different from retraining last few layers which is what most state of the art methods do?"
Ans: The key difference between our architecture and other architecture where the last layers are retrained is that, in our architecture, the class-specific models in "level 1" need not be a neural network. A random forest trained to recognize a particular class can be used as well. This allows the user to create highly computationally efficient class-specific models. However, in the traditional architectures, the previous layers are perceptron/neural layers. We benchmarked our model against Fixed expansion layer (FEL) network which is one such network and demonstrated that our model outperforms such architectures. Please refer to Table 2 row number 4 for the benchmarking results. Our proposed architecture outperforms FEL in both base knowledge retention capacity and overall knowledge retention capacity by a large margin. We also benchmarked our architecture against Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) which also involves updating only specific paths in a neural network. Please refer to Table 2 row number 2 for comparison results. Our model outperformed EWC on new knowledge and overall knowledge retention capabilities.

4. "As per description only a fraction of points from the rest of the classes are utilized as negative examples for learning a given class? This fraction seems very important/sensitive? What is its influence in evaluations?"
Ans: We agree that the fraction of points selected might influence the performance of the architecture, however choosing a random fraction of points was enough to get state of the art performance. We plan to study the effects of the chosen samples on the performance of the architecture in future work.

5. "  When a new class comes in in the form of incremental learning, one needs to retrain all the class-specific models! "
Ans: This is not true. We are not retraining all the class-specific models on the new class data. Only the classifier in the second level is being retrained. That is the reason we called it as "partial rehearsal". Please refer to Algorithm 1 for clarification.  

6. "How is this small rehearsal or how is this different from retraining like in the conventional case?"
Ans: We wanted to show that retraining only the classifier in the final level of the architecture is enough to retain the base knowledge while the classifiers in level 1 will retain the new knowledge. We demonstrated that our approach is better than retraining the entire network in Table 4. We benchmarked our proposed architecture against a CNN which was allowed to rehearse the old data. Table 4 clearly shows our model outperforming the "overall retraining of the neural network" concept.

Thank you.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper presents an approach to avoiding catastrophic forgetting in neural networks trained on classification tasks in an incremental manner. The authors term their approach “EnsembleNet”. The approach is very straightforward: the network architecture utilizes one sub-network for each class that outputs an “opinion” score for an input, which indicates whether the input is a member of the class associated with that sub-network. A multi-layer perceptron then takes the opinion scores of each of the sub-networks and classifies the input. Whenever a new class is introduced, a new sub-network is trained up. The authors provide data showing that this approach does better at avoiding catastrophic forgetting than other approaches that have been proposed.

This paper was reasonably easy to read, and the motivations clear. However, it suffers from some major flaws that make its contributions quite limited, in my opinion:

1) This approach can only ever work on classification tasks where we know the correct label for the data, or tasks where there is an explicit signal of learning from a new distribution occurring. If we do not know that we are now receiving data from a new category/task, then the network has no way to accommodate the new data. In other words, this approach essentially puts all the onus on the programmer/dataset for indicating whether to use new weights or adapt old ones, unlike other approaches that try to do this in an automated manner (e.g. Kirkpatrick et al., 2017). That effectively makes the problem trivial, by assuming that the hard work has already been done. This is essentially just a standard ensemble approach. Indeed, one could take this approach to the extreme and simply train a new neural network every time data from a new class is encountered. As such, I don’t see how this paper makes any truly interesting theoretical or practical contribution to solving the problem of catastrophic forgetting.

2) The claim that there would be time savings is not well supported. First, the time savings only happen if one assumes that the training is done in parallel on different machines. But, if training of each sub-network is incremental, then it can’t be done in parallel! Moreover, the mathematical analysis in the supplementary is ridden with errors. Aside from numerous typos and errors in writing (see for example the equations at the bottom of page 10, or the broken equation reference on page 11), the basic analysis is wrong in several places, from what I can tell. Consider, “Lemma” 7.1.3: the authors start by assuming alpha <=1, they then demonstrate that this can work for any value of c or |S|, since -4*c/|S| < 0 for all c and |S| > 0. Fine, but that doesn’t prove that alpha <= 1! All that shows is that if alpha <= 1 it does not lead to a contradiction. Indeed, they can’t assume that alpha <=1, because alpha is how the training time scales with the number of datapoints, and there is zero guarantee that this is sublinear. From what I can tell, the “proof” that T_en<T_ord is, in fact, invalid.

Some slightly more minor points:

- Critical measures like Omega_new, alpha_ideal, etc. should be defined, at least in the supplemental, not left for readers to go and look up in another paper.

- I am not convinced that the benchmarking results from Kemker et al. (2018) provide fair comparisons. How well were these networks optimized in that work? Did EWC really only achieve 0.001 for Omega_new? That strikes me as potentially a hyperparameter tuning problem.

- Figure 4 seems to tell us nothing beyond the easily stated: we can train each sub-network on a different computer (but, see my first major point above).

- Is the final classifier only trained after all the sub-networks have been trained? That’s what Algorithm 1 seems to imply. In which case, it’s not truly incremental training!

Altogether, given these various considerations, I cannot recommend this paper for publication at ICLR.

display_title: Thank you for your careful review, we request you to consider the arguments that we present in our defence.

content.title: Thank you for your careful review, we request you to consider the arguments that we present in our defence.
content.comment:
1. "This approach can only ever work on classification tasks where we know the correct label for the data, or tasks where there is an explicit signal of learning from a new distribution occurring. If we do not know that we are now receiving data from a new category/task, then the network has no way to accommodate the new data."
Ans: This is true for even widely accepted architectures like CNN and not just our architecture. Our aim is to mitigate catastrophic forgetting in a supervised learning scenario which is commonly experienced by important architectures like ANNs and CNNs.

2. " In other words, this approach essentially puts all the onus on the programmer/dataset for indicating whether to use new weights or adapt old ones"
Ans: Since our proposed architecture is working in supervised setting, the arival of a new sample that belongs to new class is straightforward to detect. Our model is capable of detecting arrival of point belonging to new class and automatically creating a new model to accomidate the new class. Please see line number 11 in Algorithm 1. EnsembleNet checks whether the newly arrived point belongs to previously known classes. If the point belongs to a new class, then a new model is automatically created. No intervention by programmer is required.

3. " Indeed, one could take this approach to the extreme and simply train a new neural network every time data from a new class is encountered."
Ans: Our architecture only requires partial rehearsal. i.e.. only the classifier present in the final level is retrained. This requires less computational time compared to creating a new model and training it on entire new data everytime. We demonstrated that the proposed architecture demonstrates higher knowledge retention capacities and faster training times compared to retraining the entire network in Table 4. 

4. " As such, I don’t see how this paper makes any truly interesting theoretical or practical contribution to solving the problem of catastrophic forgetting."
Ans: Our work demonstrates that the Stability-Plasticity dilemma can be balanced using a relatively simple architecture like our own. The neural networks in the first level remain untouched when new class data comes which contributes to the stability of the model and the final classifier is retrained which contributes to the plasticity of the model. Please read the DISCUSSION section of the paper where we discussed this in little more detail. Even though our proposed architecture is simple and can be roughly compared to other architectures like StackingC, the minor changes that we propose were enough to achieve state of the art performance. If you see Table 2, EnsembleNet outperformed every other architecture which are much more complicated. EnsembleNet demonstrated atleast 0.92 on almost all $\Omega$ values despite its simple architecture. 

5. " The claim that there would be time savings is not well supported."
Ans: Please refer to Table 4 where we tabulated experimental results demonstrating that EnsembleNet trains faster than traditional CNN. $T_{F}$ represents the total training time of the model. Please note that EnsembleNet required only 112 seconds while other models required 180 seconds and 120 seconds. 

6. "But, if training of each sub-network is incremental, then it can’t be done in parallel! "
Ans: When a new sub-network is being trained on a new class, the sub-network can be trained on a different machine parallelly without disturbing the current model. After the new sub-network has been trained, it can be appended to the current model. Parallel architectures can be utilized even during the prediction phase. When a point is being classified by the sub-networks, all the sub-networks can run parallelly as they are not dependent on each other. 

7. "Moreover, the mathematical analysis in the supplementary is ridden with errors"
Ans: Thank you for your review. We will make the necessary changes before the final date or remove it from the supplementary section if we run short of time.

8. "Critical measures like Omega_new, alpha_ideal, etc. should be defined, at least in the supplemental"
Ans: Thank you for the advice. We will add it in the supplementary.

9. "I am not convinced that the benchmarking results from Kemker et al. (2018) provide fair comparisons. How well were these networks optimized in that work? Did EWC really only achieve 0.001 for Omega_new? That strikes me as potentially a hyperparameter tuning problem.
"
Ans: With all due respect, there was no hyperparameter tuning problem with EWC. EWC is more suitable for multi-modal learning as demonstrated by the same Kemker et al. (2018) paper. When EWC was tasked with incrementally learning CUB200 and CIFAR100, it was one of the top performers.

10. "Is the final classifier only trained after all the sub-networks have been trained?"
Ans: We did not understand the concern. Can you please repeat the concern so that we can better address it?

Thank you.
